Normally, that would be a cut-and-dried case. But there's case-law precedent that makes this a rather sticky topic, and is an excellent case study in how case law complicates normally-black-and-white issues.

McFall v Shimp is a case where Shimp was the sole viable donor for bone marrow for McFall. Robert McFall had fallen ill to a very treatable form of bone marrow disease called "aplastic anemia", and it would have easily been treated with a bone marrow transplant. The procedure had anywhere from a 65-85% success probability (numbers vary, according to source) of entirely curing his disorder. Unfortunately, the only viable donor was his first cousin, David Shimp. Unfortunately for McFall, Shimp refused to donate marrow. So McFall took Shimp to court in an attempt to force Shimp to donate marrow for his benefit. This touched off a debate in the courts over whether or not the State could be invoked to coerce someone to submit to medical procedures for another's primary benefit, namely the use of their body for another's primary benefit (Which I think we can both agree, regardless of our stances on abortion, even if we grant the Fetal personhood argument, that the Fetus is the primary beneficiary of any policy outlawing abortive procedures).

The courts ultimately sided against forcing Shimp to donate his marrow for McFall's benefit, and McFall passed away approx two weeks from a massive hemorrhage after his case was decided against him, establishing the precedent that it is unconstitutional to use the State to coerce one individual to provide the use of their body for the benefit of another, due to the violation of personal autonomy any such policy engenders. If we grant the Fetal Personhood argument, and consider the Rights of the Woman on the same level as the Rights of the Fetus, anyone concerned about the overreach of Big Government should be wary of wanting to revoke the protections set by the case law precedent of McFall v Shimp, due to the "rule which would know no limits", to quote Presiding Judge John P. Flaherty on the case law in question, it would open up.

So despite being an AnCap/Libertarian I'm also very intrigued by the idea of basic income.

Both Friedman and Hayek advocated for a basic income.

On Basic Income, Friedman has said: "We should replace the ragbag of welfare programs with a single, comprehensive program of income supplements in cash"

He also advocated for abolishing the Federal Reserve, and I think that it makes sense to do both.

I've always been in favor of abolishing the Federal Reserve and substituting a machine program that would keep the quantity of money going up at a steady rate.

If you really carried out the logic concerning the quantity of money, you deprive the Federal Reserve of anything to do. Suppose the Federal Reserve said it was going to increase the quantity of money by 4 percent a year, year after year, week after week, month after month. That would be a purely mechanical project. You could program a computer to do that.

  • Friedman

4% of M3 comes to about 3 trillion dollars: http://gizmodo.com/5995301/how-much-money-is-there-on-earth

This (3 trillion) is commonly cited as a rough figure for how much a significant American UBI would cost.

Hayek was a big proponent of digital currency, and I think a cryptocurrency like Bitcoin is exactly the sort of system that could implement Friedman's vision and replace the Federal Reserve.

I don't believe we shall ever have a good money again before we take the thing out of the hands of government, that is, we can't take them violently out of the hands of government, all we can do is by some sly roundabout way introduce something that they can't stop.
